subject: Clarify: geolocation telemetry and CCPA/CPRA service provider boundary
messages:
From: Aaron Cho <aaron@greengrid.io>
To: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-30T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Geolocation telemetry — CCPA/CPRA classification and DPA redlines

Hi Mina / Ben,

Thanks for taking a look at this. We ran into a question in Legal about how Greengrid's location telemetry would be treated under CCPA/CPRA if we contract with Redwood as a service provider. We have two product flows: 

- "Aggregated footfall" — county-level counts derived from device pings (no persistent user-id shared, thresholds applied).
- "Proximity notifications" — push notifications triggered when a user enters a geofence; triggers are evaluated server-side against a device identifier (hashed id).

Our in-house counsel flagged the proximity workflow as potentially a "sale" under CCPA if it enables targeted messaging, which would disqualify us from labeling Redwood a service provider for that traffic. We're trying to avoid a wholesale change in our architecture but will if we must.

Attached are our current DPA redlines (Greengrid_DPA_redlines_v3.pdf). Two asks from Legal: (1) can Redwood confirm whether precise lat/long telemetry used for proximity counts would be treated as personal information that could be "sold" under CCPA when used for targeted notifications? (2) if Redwood is a service provider, what subprocessor controls / notice windows can you provide for third parties that process geolocation (e.g., mapping, geofence vendors)?

High level: we want to keep the aggregated flow as "service provider" friendly, and if proximity is problematic we want options for coarse-grain evaluation or on-device matching. Happy to set up a quick sync.

Best,
Aaron
Legal — Greengrid Inc.

Subject: Re: Geolocation telemetry — CCPA/CPRA classification and DPA redlines

Hi Aaron — thanks for the clear context and for sending the redlines. Quick summary up front: precise location tied to persistent identifiers will generally be treated as "personal information" under CCPA/CPRA; whether processing constitutes a "sale" depends on the purpose (advertising/monetization vs. analytics) and the contract restrictions. Below I outline practical paths and contract language we can offer to keep Redwood strictly in a service-provider role for both flows where possible.

1) Aggregated footfall (county-level)
- If you provide only sufficiently aggregated, thresholded counts with no device-level identifiers or reversible hashes, we can accept that as limited-use telemetry (service provider). Our standard Exhibit A allows delivery of aggregated metrics; we'll propose an explicit deidentification threshold and a maximum granularity clause (e.g., county or 0.1-degree bins).

2) Proximity notifications (server-side triggers)
- This is trickier. If you send us device identifiers to evaluate triggers and we return a user-specific action/targeting signal used for promotional messages, many counsel teams (and regulators) view that as behaviorally targeted communications, which can fall under the CCPA "sale" definition.
- Contract levers we can offer: 
  a) Explicit Limited Use: Redwood will only use location telemetry to provide the requested trigger evaluation and will not use it for advertising, profiling, or enrichment.
  b) No Resale / No Onward Transfer for Advertising: a strict prohibition on Redwood transferring location-derived signals for advertising or resale; downstream transfers only permitted to subprocessors listed in Exhibit B and only for the processing purposes set forth.
  c) Subprocessor Controls: 30-day notice for new subprocessors + right to object for specific high-risk vendors + SOC 2 + subprocessor attestation for location processors.
  d) On-device / pseudonymous option: if Greengrid hashes the trigger logic client-side and only sends opaque tokens we match, that reduces sale risk. We can support integration patterns (edge matching) that avoid raw IDs reaching our servers.

3) Retention & Deletion
- We'll accept a strict retention window for location telemetry used for proximity triggers (e.g., 30 days) with immediate deletion on request or on contract termination for customer data, documented in the DPA Exhibit.

4) Evidence & Audit
- We can supply SOC 2 Type II report and provide the subprocessor list. For geolocation providers we rely on (e.g., mapping vendor), we'll produce attestation templates.

Next steps: I'll have our legal team convert the bullet points above into redline language for your DPA draft. I'll attach a short draft exhibit with targeted clauses for location telemetry and subprocessor notice (redwood-DPA-exhibit-location-clauses-draft.docx). If you'd like, Ben and I can join a 30-minute call to walk Legal through the on-device vs server-side tradeoffs.

Regards,

Aaron — thanks for flagging. Mina's summary is spot-on. A couple of practical notes from Sales/Customer success: 

- If proximity triggers force Greengrid into a "seller" posture, that could materially change pricing and the contractual model.
- Workaround we see working in practice: coarse-grain hashes (city/county level) or on-device evaluation. Both keep the product intact for many customers and maintain SP treatment.
- If you want, we can propose two lanes in the SOW: (1) Server-side proximity with stricter contract controls and a higher price band; (2) On-device/coarse lane with standard SP economics.

I'll loop in Karthik for whether any engineering constraints on latency/cost would block an on-device flow.

Best,

Subject: Re: Geolocation telemetry — CCPA/CPRA classification and DPA redlines

Aaron / team — Marissa from Legal here. Appreciate the clear background. A few concrete redline asks from our side to make Redwood's position as a service provider defensible and to limit downstream exposure: 

1) No Sale / No Advertising: Add an explicit clause that Redwood will not (and will not permit subprocessors to) sell, transfer, or otherwise enable the targeted advertising or personalized marketing of individuals using the location telemetry it processes. This should include a prohibition on using location-derived signals to build advertising profiles or to enrich third-party audience segments.

2) Subprocessor Exhibit: We require an Exhibit B listing current subprocessors. New subprocessors that process location telemetry require 30-day notice and a documented attestation (SOC 2 or equivalent) before they can be used for location processing. If Greengrid objects to a specific subprocessor on reasonable security/privacy grounds, the parties will meet to discuss alternatives.

3) Data Minimization & Granularity Caps: For aggregated analytics, contract should specify the maximum granularity (county or larger) and minimum cohort size (e.g., at least 5 devices per bucket) before reporting.

4) Retention & Deletion SLA: For proximity triggers, we want a maximum retention of 30 days unless otherwise agreed in writing. Deletion requests from data subjects must be honored within 30 days, and we will provide export/deletion evidence on request.

5) Technical Safeguards: Encryption at rest and in transit (TLS1.2+), customer-managed KMS option for keys used to persist identifiers, and clear logging/audit trail linking access to specific subprocessors.

6) Remedy for Non-Compliance: Limited right to audit relevant processing and requirement to remediate high-risk subprocessor findings within a defined timeframe (e.g., 30 days).

I've attached a subprocessor attestation template that we can use for any mapping/geofence vendors (subprocessor_attestation_template.pdf). We'll produce a DPA redline incorporating (1)-(6) and share a comment-ready draft.

If Greengrid prefers, we can schedule a focused 45-minute call w/ Product, Sales, and Legal to walk through the options and the SOW lanes Ben proposed. Please propose times.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
